label: SES-405 — Application generation test: Mentor Application against the prototype; writing standards move into the system

conversation.conversation_title: Can CRM Builder build the Mentor Application from its process definition?
conversation.conversation_purpose: Test how close CRM Builder can come to the running cbm-client-intake application from the Mentor Application process definition alone, and record the changes the system needs to support application generation.
conversation.conversation_description: Seed prompt: "Please review the process object in crmbuilder v2 - cleveland business mentoring - proc-001 Mentor application. Based on this information, I would like to have an architectural discussion on how we could develop a custom application that uses the CRM as a backend, that would automate this process." The conversation established that the CBM client applications were hand-built prototypes and that the exercise is a comparison of CRM Builder's reach against them. Three framings were tried in turn: a runtime engine that interprets the definition, deterministic code generation, and the one the product owner ruled — an AI agent that builds and maintains the application from the definition, with a technical user operating it. A gap register was produced in three drafts. The product owner then required that all output be readable by a technical, non-expert reader, and that this rule live inside CRM Builder rather than on his personal wiki, so that the rules travel with the system to any user. The three writing standards are migrated into system-scope governance rules and the two existing rules that name the product owner by name are generalised.
conversation.conversation_summary: Ruled: CRM Builder holds the definition and an AI agent builds, tests, deploys and maintains the application; the writing standards become system-scope governance rules with the person named as a role. Produced: the application-generation gap register (v0.3), fifteen planning items for the CRMBUILDER engagement, four new governance rules and two amended ones.
conversation.conversation_executive_summary: The Mentor Application process definition is a good description of a business process and a poor specification of an application. CRM Builder cannot yet produce the prototype from it. The agent-generation model is ruled, the gaps are registered as planning items, and the writing standards move into the system as governance rules so they reach every session on every surface.

session.session_title: Application generation test: the Mentor Application against the prototype, and the writing standards move into the system
session.session_description: Claude.ai Cowork session, 2026-09-05. Reviewed the Mentor Application process (PROC-001 in the Cleveland Business Mentors engagement) and the prototype cbm-client-intake application, and asked whether CRM Builder could produce the application from the definition alone. Produced the application-generation gap register, ruled the agent-generation model, and moved the writing standards into system-scope governance rules.
session.session_executive_summary: CRM Builder cannot yet build the Mentor Application from its definition: the definition describes the business process well but is silent on the form, the screens, failure behaviour and access. The product owner ruled that an AI agent builds the application from the definition. Sixteen gaps in three layers were registered and fifteen become planning items. The writing standards become system-scope governance rules so the rules travel with the system.
session.session_notes: In flight at end: two rulings belong to the Cleveland Business Mentors engagement, not this one — whether a person or the application moves a candidate to Provisional (the definition and the prototype disagree), and the fill policy for a repeat applicant's existing record. Next step: rule the Provisional question, then write the transition table and the field roles for the Mentor Application.

planning_items.title: A transition record type: one row per allowed status move, with actor, required fields and automatic actions
planning_items.description: An application needs one list of allowed status moves: from which value to which, who may make the move, what must be filled in first, and what happens automatically afterward. Today that list can only be assembled from a process's prose steps and several decisions, and two regenerations would assemble it differently. Add a transition record type on the process, referencing the entity and its status field, and let views, screens, automations and conformance tests refer to individual transitions. Source: gap GAP-01 in the application-generation gap register.
planning_items.executive_summary: Add a transition record type so a process's status lifecycle is stated once, as data, and everything else can refer to it. Each row names the move from one status value to another, who may make it, which fields must be filled in first, and what happens automatically afterward. Views, screens, automations and conformance tests then refer to individual transitions instead of reassembling the lifecycle from prose steps and decisions. Source: gap GAP-01 in the application-generation gap register.

planning_items.title: A role on each process-to-field link: collected by form, edited by persona, set by system, or display only
planning_items.description: The process-to-field link says only that a process touches a field. An application needs to know whether the field is typed into a public form, edited by a team member during the process, set by the system, or shown read-only, and for form fields, in what order and grouping. Without the role a builder has to guess from field names. Add the role, order and group attributes to the link. Source: GAP-02.
planning_items.executive_summary: Add a role and ordering to process-to-field links so forms and screens can be derived from them. Today the link says only that a process touches a field. The role states whether the field is typed into a public form, edited by a team member during the process, set by the system, or shown read-only; for form fields the link also carries the order and grouping. Without this a builder has to guess from field names. Source: GAP-02.

planning_items.title: A form record type: field set, validation, value mapping, file handling, spam protection and submitter messages
planning_items.description: Nothing in the definition describes a public form. The prototype form has required fields, option lists, a resume upload, a hidden bot-trap field, one consent checkbox that writes six yes/no fields across two records, a message per outcome, and a mapping from submitted data onto two CRM records. Add a form record type owning the collected field set (from PI-472), per-field validation, one-to-many value mapping, file handling, spam protection and the messages the submitter sees on success, refusal and error. Source: GAP-03.
planning_items.executive_summary: Add a form record type so a public form can be built from the definition instead of invented. The record owns the collected field set, per-field validation, one-to-many value mapping onto CRM records, file handling, spam protection and the messages the submitter sees on success, refusal and error. Nothing in the definition describes a public form today; the prototype's form carries all of these. Source: GAP-03.

planning_items.title: Automation records carry a precondition, a confirmation condition and a failure behaviour
planning_items.description: The definition names automatic actions (thank-you email, conflict notification, mailbox creation, login creation) but not what each needs before it runs, how success is confirmed, or what happens when it fails. The prototype encodes all three: the status moves only once the mailbox is confirmed; a failed group membership is reported but does not block; a missing mailbox blocks approval when creation is off. Extend the automation record type with these three attributes so outage-time behaviour is stated, not decided by the builder. Source: GAP-05.
planning_items.executive_summary: Extend automation records with a precondition, a confirmation condition and a failure behaviour so a rebuilt application behaves the same on a bad day. The definition names automatic actions but not what each needs before it runs, how success is confirmed, or what happens when it fails; the prototype encodes all three. Stating them in the record removes the builder's guesswork about outage-time behaviour. Source: GAP-05.

planning_items.title: An external system record type: the systems an application talks to, their capabilities and their settings
planning_items.description: The prototype talks to the CRM, a directory service for mailboxes and groups, an email sender and the website, each with credentials and settings. CRM Builder records individual settings but has no record for an external system. Add a record naming the system, the capabilities used (check a mailbox exists, create one, manage groups, send mail), the settings each capability needs, and a test-connection requirement. Automation records reference it. This is the one place product names belong. Source: GAP-06.
planning_items.executive_summary: Add an external system record type so automations can name what they talk to and what they need. The record names the system, the capabilities used (check a mailbox exists, create one, manage groups, send mail), the settings each capability needs, and a test-connection requirement. Automation records reference it. This is the one place product names belong. Source: GAP-06.

planning_items.title: A screen record type: list or detail screens composed of views, field groups, transition actions and bulk actions, scoped to a persona
planning_items.description: The definition describes one filtered list. The prototype's staff tool has a searchable roster with computed columns, a detail screen with a summary card and a tabbed editor, transition buttons, a separate save for permission groups, and a bulk sweep. Add a screen record type built from views, the field groups of PI-472, the transitions of PI-471 and bulk actions, each screen tied to the persona that uses it. This is the gap where two rebuilds would differ most. Source: GAP-07.
planning_items.executive_summary: Add a screen record type so what a team sees is defined, not improvised. A screen is a list or detail screen composed of views, the field groups of the process-to-field links, the transitions of the transition record type and bulk actions, and is tied to the persona that uses it. This is the gap where two rebuilds of the same application would differ most. Source: GAP-07.

planning_items.title: A process-artifact pattern: notes typed by process step and a decision record per transition
planning_items.description: The Mentor Application requires each reviewer's written opinion, a decision summary per vote (outcome, date, decline reason) and a provisional-period checklist. The checklist items are fields; the opinions and decision summaries exist nowhere. Rather than model them per engagement, add a general pattern that the builder applies automatically at every transition: a note attached to a process step, and a decision record attached to a transition. Source: GAP-10.
planning_items.executive_summary: Add a general pattern for review notes and per-transition decision records that the builder applies automatically at every transition: a note attached to a process step and a decision record attached to a transition. The Mentor Application requires reviewer opinions and a decision summary per vote, and these exist nowhere in the definition today; a general pattern avoids modelling them per engagement. Source: GAP-10.

planning_items.title: Execution identity and admission rule on every screen and automation action
planning_items.description: The prototype runs every read and write as the signed-in user so the CRM enforces permissions, except creating a login, which runs under an administrator service account; access to the tool is limited to one team. The definition has personas and roles but says nothing about which actions run as whom or which team membership opens which screen. Add an execution identity (signed-in user or service account) and an admission rule (persona or team) to screens (PI-476) and automation actions (PI-474). Source: GAP-11.
planning_items.executive_summary: State who each screen and action runs as, and who may reach it. Add an execution identity (the signed-in user or a service account) and an admission rule (a persona or a team) to screen records and automation actions. The prototype runs most work as the signed-in user so the CRM enforces permissions, with one privileged action under a service account, and limits the tool to one team; the definition says none of this today. Source: GAP-11.

planning_items.title: An application-builder agent profile and skill
planning_items.description: CRM Builder stores agent profiles, skills and governance rules and loads them into sessions, but has no profile for the agent that builds an application. Define one: what it reads from the definition and in what order (process, transitions, forms, screens, automations, external systems, access, the kernel contract), what it produces, what it may not decide on its own, and a standing rule that any behaviour the definition does not state is raised as a planning item rather than invented. Source: GAP-12.
planning_items.executive_summary: Define the agent that builds applications from definitions: an agent profile and skill stating what it reads from the definition and in what order, what it produces, what it may not decide on its own, and a standing rule that any behaviour the definition does not state is raised as a planning item rather than invented. CRM Builder stores agent profiles and rules today but has no profile for this agent. Source: GAP-12.

planning_items.title: Extract the application kernel from cbm-client-intake into a versioned library with a written contract
planning_items.description: The prototype contains the runtime every generated application needs identically: capture to the application's own database before the CRM is touched, a file-queue fallback (required, not yet built), an idempotent delivery worker, a receipt record, reconciliation sweeps, CRM sign-in passthrough with a service account for privileged actions, option-value drift tolerance, phone normalisation, attachments, template email sending, and an encrypted settings store with test-connection actions. Extract it into a library with a contract stating how a form registers, how a transition is declared and how an automation names an external system, so the builder produces only the process-specific layer. Largest item in the register; size unverified. Source: GAP-13 and Layer 3.
planning_items.executive_summary: Turn the prototype's generic runtime into a reusable kernel the builder composes rather than rebuilds. Extract the capture-first storage, file-queue fallback, idempotent delivery worker, receipts, reconciliation sweeps, CRM sign-in passthrough, drift tolerance, phone normalisation, attachments, template email and encrypted settings store into a versioned library with a written contract. Largest item in the register; size unverified. Source: GAP-13 and Layer 3.

planning_items.title: Conformance tests generated from the definition
planning_items.description: Nothing checks that a built application does what its definition says. Generate a test specification from the definition — one case per transition, per repeat-applicant branch, per automation precondition and failure path, per form outcome message — that the application must pass before deployment. This is what makes rebuilding from a changed definition safe. The verification-specification generator skeleton for CRM configuration is the starting point. Source: GAP-14.
planning_items.executive_summary: Generate behaviour tests from the definition so a rebuild can be checked, not trusted. The test specification carries one case per transition, per repeat-applicant branch, per automation precondition and failure path, and per form outcome message, and the application must pass it before deployment. The verification-specification generator skeleton for CRM configuration is the starting point. Source: GAP-14.

planning_items.title: Every generated module, test and screen carries the identifiers of the definition records it realises
planning_items.description: The prototype cites decisions in code comments by hand and inconsistently. Add a rule, and the builder behaviour behind it, that generated code, tests and screens name the process, transition, form, view, automation and requirement they implement, so a definition change can be traced to the code it affects and a rebuild reviewed as a diff against the definition. Source: GAP-15.
planning_items.executive_summary: Trace every generated artifact back to the definition records it implements. Add the rule, and the builder behaviour behind it, that generated code, tests and screens name the process, transition, form, view, automation and requirement they realise, so a definition change can be traced to the code it affects and a rebuild reviewed as a diff against the definition. Source: GAP-15.

planning_items.title: A regeneration protocol: what happens when a definition changes
planning_items.description: The prototype is maintained by prompting. Write the procedure for bringing an application back into line after its definition changes: which records changed, which code is affected (PI-482), which tests must run again (PI-481), how the technical user approves the change, and how it is deployed. Record it as a process in this engagement, executed by the agent profile of PI-479. Source: GAP-16.
planning_items.executive_summary: Define the procedure that keeps a built application in step with its definition: which records changed, which code is affected, which tests must run again, how the technical user approves the change, and how it is deployed. Record it as a process in this engagement, executed by the application-builder agent profile. The prototype is maintained by prompting today. Source: GAP-16.

planning_items.title: One bootstrap call on the MCP server returns the effective governance rules and the agent contract
planning_items.description: Claude Code sessions load the effective rules through a session-start hook; build agents resolve them through their profile contract; a chat or Cowork session gets them only if project instructions tell it to read them. For the rules to reach any surface for any user with no outside instructions, add a single bootstrap tool on the MCP server that returns the effective rules for the active engagement and the requested agent profile's contract in one call. Raised when the writing standards moved into the system.
planning_items.executive_summary: Let any session on any surface load the rules with one call and no outside instructions. Add a single bootstrap tool on the MCP server that returns the effective governance rules for the active engagement and the requested agent profile's contract together. Today Claude Code sessions get the rules from a start hook and chat sessions only if project instructions say to read them. Raised when the writing standards moved into the system.

planning_items.title: A check kind for prose: reject a reply or document that cites a record identifier without saying what it means
planning_items.description: Enforced rules are checked today by a hook that evaluates a shell command against a predicate before it runs; the check kinds are forbidden command, required trailer and protected path. Writing rules have no check. Add a check kind that scans a reply or a document for bare identifiers (a DEC, REQ, FLD, PROC or similar identifier not inside parentheses) and, in Claude Code, returns the reply with the rule named. This is a regular-expression check: it catches the cited pattern and nothing subtler, and has no equivalent on chat surfaces, where the rule stays advisory. Raised when the plain-language rule was created.
planning_items.executive_summary: Make the plain-language writing rule enforceable in Claude Code with a prose check. Add a check kind that scans a reply or a document for bare record identifiers not inside parentheses and returns the reply with the rule named. This is a regular-expression check: it catches the cited pattern and nothing subtler, and has no equivalent on chat surfaces, where the rule stays advisory. Raised when the plain-language rule was created.

decisions.title: CRM Builder holds the definition; an AI agent builds, tests, deploys and maintains the application; a technical user operates it
decisions.context: The session asked whether CRM Builder could produce the Mentor Application application from its process definition. Two framings were put by the assistant: a runtime engine that interprets the definition, and deterministic code generation whose output is never hand-edited. The product owner set both aside.
decisions.decision: The generator is an AI agent. CRM Builder holds the definition. The agent reads it and writes, tests, deploys and maintains the application code, acting as the development and operations manager. A technical user runs the agent, approves changes and holds credentials, but does not develop the application. Generated code is never hand-edited in a way that must survive regeneration; anything the definition cannot express is fixed in CRM Builder, not in the code. Every generated application shares a common kernel built once and reused.
decisions.rationale: The product owner's ruling, on evidence: the cbm-client-intake application has run in production for months, built and maintained exactly this way.
decisions.alternatives_considered: A runtime engine interpreting the definition (rejected: it is also code someone must hold, and it front-loads five record types before any screen appears). Deterministic code generation (rejected as the wrong reading of the goal: the builder is an agent working from the definition, not an emitter).
decisions.consequences: The test of a definition becomes whether it says everything the application must do, completely and unambiguously, so that two builds behave the same and can be checked. The gap register is re-scoped on that test. The application-builder agent profile, the kernel, conformance tests, traceability and a regeneration protocol become planning items in this engagement.
decisions.executive_summary: The product owner ruled (2026-09-05) that CRM Builder holds the definition and an AI agent builds and maintains the application from it, with a technical user operating; the prototype proves the model.

decisions.title: The application-generation test is run per process against the prototype and recorded as a gap register
decisions.context: The CBM client applications were hand-built prototypes to learn what such an application must do. The product owner is feeding the learned requirements back into CRM Builder to see how close the system can come to an already running system from the same requirements, and asked for the changes needed to support application generation.
decisions.decision: One fully defined process at a time is compared against the prototype that implements it, and the result is a gap register in three layers: what the definition cannot yet say, what the builder needs beyond the definition, and what the shared kernel must contain. The first register covers the Mentor Application and is committed under specifications/application-generation/ in the crmbuilder repository. Each gap becomes a planning item in this engagement; content gaps in the client's definition go to the client's engagement.
decisions.rationale: A per-process comparison against running code is the only measure that does not depend on opinion. The prototype is the ground truth for what the application must do.
decisions.alternatives_considered: A general capability review of CRM Builder without a reference application (rejected: no ground truth).
decisions.consequences: The Mentor Application register v0.3 is the first record. Two items it raised are rulings for the Cleveland Business Mentors engagement, not this one: whether a person or the application moves a candidate to Provisional, and the fill policy for a repeat applicant's existing record. The next process registers reuse the same three layers.
decisions.executive_summary: The product owner set the method (2026-09-05): compare each fully defined process against the prototype that runs it and record the gaps in a three-layer register, each gap becoming a planning item in this engagement. The Mentor Application register is the first record.

decisions.title: The writing standards live in CRM Builder as system-scope governance rules; a person named in a rule is named as a role
decisions.context: The product owner required that all output be readable by a technical but non-expert reader: never cite a record identifier as if the reader knew what it meant. He then ruled that this cannot live on his personal wiki, which is his own way of working with Claude: CRM Builder must contain everything, including agent definitions and rules, so that the rules are transferable to any user of the system with very little outside information. Reading the 241 governance rules showed that a fragment of the rule already existed, scoped to approval requests in Claude Code only, and that the existing rules name the product owner personally.
decisions.decision: Four system-scope governance rules are created, audience all sessions, applying always: plain language for the reader; executive register; terminology precision; reply format. The three standards are migrated from the wiki with the person named as the product owner. The two existing rules that name the product owner by name (the terminology governance rule and the approval-request communication rule) are amended to say the product owner. The wiki remains the product owner's personal mirror and is not a source for the system. Enforcement is advisory until a prose check kind exists.
decisions.rationale: A system that cannot write for its reader without one user's wiki fails the transferability test the product owner set. The governance-rule table already reaches Claude Code sessions at start and build agents through their contracts.
decisions.alternatives_considered: Adding the single plain-language rule and leaving the three standards on the wiki (rejected by the product owner's recommendation-accepted ruling: quick, but the system would still depend on the wiki).
decisions.consequences: Four rule records created and two amended by the apply prompt for this session. Two copies of each standard exist until the wiki mirrors are retired. A bootstrap tool on the MCP server and a prose check kind become planning items so the rules reach every surface and can be enforced where a hook exists.
decisions.executive_summary: The product owner ruled (2026-09-05) that the writing standards become system-scope governance rules inside CRM Builder, with people named as roles, so the rules travel with the system to any user; the wiki stays a personal mirror.
